rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hijr and Sad accounts foreground Iblis’s disobedience and enmity toward humanity, omitting Adam himself; their purpose is to warn people of Iblis’s lasting hostility.
rows.anchor: فكأن الغرض من ذكر القصة في الحجر و (ص) تحذير الجنس البشري من عداوة إبليس الأبدية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the accounts share most of their wording, each has differences chosen to fit its surah’s context.
rows.anchor: إن كثيراً من الألفاظ والعبارات متطابقة في القصتين غير أن هناك اختلافاً بينهما أيضاً يتناسب وسياق كل قصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ṣalṣāl suits al-Hijr’s opening letters: it contains ṣād and alif-lām, whose combined repetitions in the story outnumber ṣād; Sad instead says ṭīn.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا يكون وضع الكلمة في السورة المبدوءة بالألف واللام أنسب، لأن مجمع ترددهما أكثر من الصاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hijr repeats ṣalṣāl in the story because the story follows the verse that already describes humanity’s creation from ṣalṣāl and dark mud.
rows.anchor: إن القصة في سورة الحجر وردت بعد قوله تعالى: {وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا الإنسان مِن صَلْصَالٍ مِّنْ حَمَإٍ مَّسْنُونٍ}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abā means refusal, while istakbara means deeming oneself superior; al-Hijr develops refusal and Sad develops arrogance.
rows.anchor: فإن معنى (أبى) : رفض وامتنع. ومعنى (استكبر) : رأى نفسه خيراً من الآخرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sad’s question about whether Iblis was arrogant or among the exalted, followed by his claim to be better than Adam, makes istakbara the fitting description; al-Aʿrāf likewise names his arrogance.
rows.anchor: ثم انظر إلى جواب إبليس في (ص) كيف كان مناسباً للاستبكار، ذلك أنه قال: {قَالَ أَنَاْ خَيْرٌ مِّنْهُ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hijr’s reply, that Iblis would not prostrate to a human made from mud, expresses refusal and abstention rather than a claim of superiority.
rows.anchor: لم يُفِدْ قولكَ الاستكبار عن فعله، ولكن يفيد الامتناع عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surrounding surah themes support the contrast: al-Hijr depicts repeated rejection, while Sad stresses arrogance through its opening, the disputants, tyrants, and mockers.
rows.anchor: ومن هذا نرى أن كل قصة وضعت في مكانها أحسن موضع وأجمله، وأن الجانب الذي عرضت له متلائم أحسن ملاءمة مع جوّ السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqara gathers the two traits separated between al-Hijr and Sad, describing Iblis as both refusing and growing arrogant.
rows.anchor: جمع فيها ما تفرق في الحجر و (ص) فقال: {إِلاَّ إِبْلِيسَ أبى واستكبر وَكَانَ مِنَ الكافرين}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hijr mentions Iblis among the prostrators because prostration is more prominent there, including the surah’s closing command; Sad instead describes David as bowing and repenting.
rows.anchor: فقد ورد السجود في قصة الحجر ست مرات، في حين ورد في قصة (ص) ثلاث مرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command for Muhammad to be among the prostrators in al-Hijr neatly contrasts with Iblis’s refusal to be among them.
rows.anchor: وهذا تناسق في التعبير جميل ومخالفة أصيلة لإبليس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sad says “my curse” after God speaks of creating Adam with His own hands, while al-Hijr uses the definite “the curse”; Sad also refers to God in the first person more often.
rows.anchor: ولما لم يكن كذلك في الحجر قال: (اللعنة)

rows.speaker: درة التنزيل
rows.claim: The cited work explains that al-Hijr’s definite “the curse” echoes its opening generic nouns, whereas Sad’s possessive “my curse” matches its direct first-person framing and the creation with God’s hands.
rows.anchor: جاء في (درة التنزيل) : "للسائل أن يسأل فيقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis swears by God’s might in Sad, matching its mention of al-ʿAzīz and its opening “in might”; in al-Hijr he invokes being led astray, matching its repeated language of misguidance.
rows.anchor: فأقسم في (ص) بعزته، وأقسم في الحجر بإغوائه، وذلك لما تقم في (ص) ذكر اسمه العزيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only al-Hijr adds Iblis’s plan to adorn earthly life, fitting that surah’s references to adornment of the sky and worldly enjoyment.
rows.anchor: فناسب ذلك ذكر التزيين في قصة الحجر دون (ص)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hijr uses the intensified form for following Satan, fitting the later promise of forgiveness and mercy: only those who follow him persistently enter the Fire; Sad’s warning is stronger.
rows.anchor: ناسب ذلك أن يخفف على عباده ويرحمهم بأن لا يدخل النار إلا من بالغ في اتباع إبليس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second contextual reason supports the gentler al-Hijr wording: the story follows reminders of blessings, while Sad’s account follows descriptions of punishment for the people of the Fire.
rows.anchor: قصة آدم في الحجر وردت بعد ذكر نعم الله على البشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distinction complements guidance promises in al-Baqara and Ṭā Hā: those verses encourage following guidance, while the Adam account warns against following Satan, joining encouragement and warning.
rows.anchor: فجمع الترغيب والترهيب في هذه القصة على أتم وأكمل صورة

rows.speaker: بعض الأعراب
rows.claim: A Bedouin criticized ending the theft passage with “forgiving, merciful”; when told it ends “mighty, wise,” he approved the wording because God imposed a decisive judgment.
rows.anchor: بعض الأعراب سمع قارئاً يقرأ: والسارق والسارقة إلى آخرها، وختمها بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mention of forgiveness or mercy does not by itself require those names to close a verse; the ending must fit the passage’s context.
rows.anchor: إنه ليس كل موطن تُذكر فيه المغفرةُ أو الرحمة، ينبغي أن تُختمَ الآيةُ بهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mumtahana 60:5 asks for forgiveness but focuses on not becoming a trial for disbelievers, so its ending “Mighty, Wise” suits the request’s main concern.
rows.anchor: ذلك لأن مَدارَ الطلب في الآية هو أنْ لا يجعلهم فتنة للذين كفروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The focal verse is set in a context where God disavows a claim made by some Christians and attributed to Jesus.
rows.anchor: إن الآية وردت في سياق التبرؤ من قولٍ قالته طائفةٌ من النصارى ونسبته إلى عيسى
